title: Simulations Overpredict Dark Matter in Heaviest Galaxies Out to 160,000 Light-Years, Study Finds
excerpt: Dark matter in galaxies is far less concentrated at the centers of massive nearby systems than galaxy simulations predict, a Nature Astronomy study of 136 galaxies reports. The gap, measured with stellar motions and FAST radio data, reaches about 160,000 light-years in the heaviest galaxies; black
content:
Massive galaxies near the Milky Way hold less dark matter at their centers than the leading cosmological simulations say they should, and the gap reaches out to about 50 kiloparsecs (about 160,000 light-years) in the heaviest systems, according to a study published in Nature Astronomy on Thursday, Nov. 26. A team led by Yu Lei of the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory analyzed 136 nearby galaxies. Modern simulations are tuned to reproduce stellar masses and star formation rates, and the authors say a comprehensive dark matter benchmark had been missing. Matching the visible galaxy, in other words, has not guaranteed matching the dark halo around it.

Shortfall Grows From 33,000 to About 160,000 Light-Years as Galaxy Mass Rises

The mismatch appears in galaxies above about 10 billion solar masses in stars, and the region where measured dark matter density falls below simulated expectations widens with stellar mass. A kiloparsec is about 3,260 light-years. The team's preprint breaks this down by mass: the low-density region extends out to about 10 kiloparsecs (about 33,000 light-years) for galaxies of roughly 10 to 30 billion solar masses, 20 to 30 kiloparsecs (about 65,000 to 98,000 light-years) for those near 30 to 100 billion, and out to about 50 kiloparsecs (about 160,000 light-years) above that, a figure the preprint treats as tentative. The full sample spans roughly 1 billion to 300 billion solar masses of stars.

Co-author Jesús Falcón-Barroso of the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC) said, "What makes this result particularly interesting is how far the discrepancy extends."

How Do Astronomers Weigh Dark Matter They Cannot See?

Dark matter gives off no light, so astronomers infer it from how fast stars and gas move under its gravity. The team used two tracers. For stars, it used integral-field velocity maps from two surveys, MaNGA (107 of the galaxies) and CALIFA (29), and fit them with a triaxial orbit-superposition model run through the public DYNAMITE code. The method assembles a model galaxy from thousands of stellar orbits, 4,410 per model in the team's validation paper, until the combined motions match the observed velocities.

Stars alone constrain mostly the inner parts of a galaxy, so the team added neutral hydrogen, which radiates at a 21-centimeter (8.3-inch) wavelength and extends farther out. Instead of mapping the gas, the method fits one integrated radio spectrum per galaxy, whose double-horned shape encodes how fast the gas rotates, and forces the gas and the stars to share one gravitational potential. The spectra came from the HI-MaNGA survey, archival single-dish data and new observations with China's 500-meter (1,640-foot) FAST radio telescope, about 12 minutes on target per galaxy, under a project the authors call PROMISE.

Joining the two datasets cuts the uncertainty on dark matter mass within 20 kiloparsecs (about 65,000 light-years) to about 30%, from about 90% with stellar motions alone. The price is modeling assumptions: the hydrogen model treats the gas as a thin, regular disk. The team began with 184 galaxies that had both kinds of data and trimmed the list to 136 after removing lopsided gas profiles, irregular stellar motions, inclinations below 35 degrees and unusually narrow hydrogen spectra. Tests on 58 mock galaxies from TNG50 showed biases in dark matter fraction of up to about 10% to 20%.

About 90% of Massive Galaxies Sit Below Simulated Median; SIMBA Deviates Furthest

The authors compared their measurements with three widely used simulation suites: IllustrisTNG (the TNG100 run), EAGLE and SIMBA. At 5 kiloparsecs (about 16,000 light-years), between 31% and 88% of galaxies across the four mass bins fall below the TNG100 one-sigma lower bound, against 16% expected if data and simulation agreed, and EAGLE's highest-mass bin reaches 97%.

Among galaxies above about 32 billion solar masses in stars, 90% have lower dark matter fractions within 20 kiloparsecs (about 65,000 light-years) than the median simulated galaxy, and 84% sit below the 16th-percentile bound. SIMBA predicts the most concentrated dark matter distributions and deviates further from the data than TNG100 or EAGLE. In a separate measure, the slope of dark matter density between 5 and 20 kiloparsecs, 74% of galaxies sit below the TNG100 median, meaning less concentrated dark matter halos.

Feedback That Cures Dwarf-Galaxy Cores Raises Dark Matter in Massive Galaxies

The paper's abstract describes a collision between two fixes. In dwarf galaxies, simulations lean on feedback from stars and black holes to ease the core–cusp problem, in which simulations build a steep central spike of dark matter while many observed dwarfs show flat centers. But the same ordinary-matter processes also pull dark matter inward in massive galaxies, steepening profiles and raising inner dark matter fractions, the opposite of what these data show. A feedback recipe that flattens dwarf cores therefore does not automatically fix massive galaxies, and may make them worse.

One proposed route to flat centers is dark matter that collides with itself. Physicists David Spergel and Paul Steinhardt proposed self-interacting dark matter in 2000 as a solution to the core–cusp problem.

Black-Hole Feedback, Self-Interacting Dark Matter and Lighter Halos Remain Unproven

The authors discuss three explanations, and none is yet established.

Energy released as matter falls onto supermassive black holes could push gas outward and reshape the dark matter around it. The authors call this plausible but untested, and note that feedback prescriptions vary widely between simulations. In a separate suite of simulations called NIHAO, galaxies above 10 billion solar masses in stars showed a growing central dark matter suppression of about 0.2 dex, roughly 40%, relative to runs without black-hole feedback. A separate analysis reports that radio-mode black-hole activity in EAGLE, SIMBA and TNG100 is inconsistent with observations.

For self-interacting dark matter, the team compared its data with AIDA-TNG, a set of runs using TNG physics with different dark matter models. A constant cross-section of 1 square centimeter per gram (about 4.4 square inches per ounce) opens low-density cores in the most massive galaxies, which is the right direction, but the cores are too small to match the observations. The authors say cores near 50 kiloparsecs (about 160,000 light-years) form only in rare halos near 100 trillion solar masses.

For the most massive galaxies, the low density could instead reflect an extended central region or a halo that is lighter or less concentrated overall. The authors say more observations are needed to tell these apart.

Does Any Independent Analysis Disagree? One Preprint Finds No Systematic Tension

A separate preprint by Pavel Mancera Piña, Justin Read and colleagues reaches a different conclusion for a different sample: 48 gas-rich galaxies and eight Milky Way satellites spanning six orders of magnitude in stellar mass, compared with the NIHAO, FIRE-2 and EDGE simulations rather than TNG100, EAGLE and SIMBA. They find no evidence of a systematic mismatch in inner dark matter density within the scope of their analysis. Their main differences are steep slopes in some massive simulated galaxies and differences in stellar-to-halo mass relations. The samples, galaxy types and simulations differ, so the two results are not a head-to-head contradiction.

The direction of the mismatch is also not the same at every scale. In June, TechTimes reported that the James Webb Space Telescope confirmed galaxy cluster XLSSC 122 has a dark matter core more concentrated than Lambda-CDM simulations predict. That is a different kind of object, observed in a different era, and the new study does not claim a shared cause.

Single-Galaxy Uncertainty Exceeds 50% While Sample Medians Hold Firm

The authors caution that for any single massive galaxy, the uncertainty on the inner dark matter fraction can exceed 50% within about 5 kiloparsecs (about 16,000 light-years). The trends are robust in the sample's medians, not in individual objects. They also list systematic uncertainties, including the degeneracy between stellar and dark mass, the assumption of a spherical halo, the assumption that stellar and gas disks are aligned, and warm and hot halo gas that cannot yet be evaluated.

Readers can check the inputs. MaNGA and CALIFA data are public, the derived masses for all 136 galaxies are in the paper's Supplementary Data, and the reduced FAST spectra are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

WEAVE-Apertif, WALLABY, MeerKAT and SKA Will Test Whether Halos Are Cored or Light

The authors present the measurements as a benchmark for future simulations that test alternative dark matter models and feedback schemes. Surveys that pair stellar and hydrogen-gas observations, such as WEAVE-Apertif, along with spatially resolved hydrogen from WALLABY, MeerKAT programs and the Square Kilometre Array, are expected to sharpen the picture. Falcón-Barroso is the principal investigator of WEAVE-Apertif, which the preprint says is expected to provide integral-field data for 400 hydrogen-resolved galaxies.

For now, the measurement gives simulation builders a number to hit: dark matter in massive nearby galaxies sits lower than the best current models say, by an amount that grows with galaxy mass to about 160,000 light-years, while black-hole feedback, simple self-interacting dark matter and lighter halos each remain unproven explanations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this prove that self-interacting dark matter is real?

No. A constant cross-section model opens cores in the right direction but too small, and a second variant, called vSIDM, does not form large cores in massive galaxies, leaving its dark matter fractions similar to standard cold dark matter.

Why do simulations that match visible galaxies still miss the dark matter?

Simulations such as TNG100 are calibrated to observed stellar masses and star formation rates. The authors say a comprehensive dark matter benchmark had been absent, and that the same ordinary-matter processes that help dwarf galaxies also compress dark matter inward in massive ones. They call the dark matter distribution of galaxies across a wide mass range a critical test for such simulations.

Does the result overturn the standard model of cosmology?

The study tests simulations built on Lambda-CDM, and the authors say the origin of the gap is unclear. In a colloquium abstract, co-author Ling Zhu wrote that important pieces of physics appear to be missing from current hydrodynamical simulations.
